title: Launch out into the deep (Luke 5:1–11)
hookLine: Peter has fished all night for nothing and lets down the nets once more

lines: A TEACHER STEPS INTO THE BOAT.
cards: Morning on the lake of Genesareth, the Sea of Galilee. Two boats pulled up on the shore, the fishermen out of them, washing their nets. Simon and his partners have worked from dark to dawn and caught nothing.
Not a small catch: nothing. They're tired, and they want to go home. Then a crowd arrives, pressing around a teacher, and the teacher steps into Simon's boat.

teach.b: Jesus asks Simon to push out a little from the land, and teaches the crowd from the boat. Then he turns to Simon and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Launch out into the deep, and let down your nets for a draught."
Simon is the expert here. He knows the lake, and he's just spent the whole night on it.

teach.h: NOTHING ALL NIGHT. BUT AT THY WORD.
teach.b: His answer is honest, and a little tired: "Master, we have laboured all the night, and have taken nothing: but at thy word I will let down the net." That but is the hinge. Not because I think it'll work.
The nets fill so full they start to break. They wave to their partners in the other boat, James and John, and both boats fill until they begin to sink. Simon doesn't celebrate.
He falls at Jesus's knees: depart from me, for I am a sinful man. The catch has frightened him, not with danger, but with nearness. Jesus answers: fear not, from now on you'll be catching people.
They bring the boats to land, leave everything, and follow him.
In the Latin Bible the line opens with three short words, duc in altum, and Pope John Paul the Second used them to open the new millennium, calling the whole Church to launch out into the deep.
Simon, of course, is the one the Church will call Peter.

how: Catholics hear this Gospel at Sunday Mass in the Lectionary's year of Luke, and "duc in altum" is a much-quoted motto since John Paul II used it in his 2001 letter for the new millennium.

games.q: you're Simon. you've fished all night and caught nothing. a teacher who isn't a fisherman tells you to go out to deep water and try again. what do you do?
o: explain politely that it won't work.
say you're tired, but you'll do it because he said so.
hand him the nets and let him try.
games.why: “Master, we have laboured all the night, and have taken nothing: but at thy word I will let down the net.” and the nets begin to break.

practice: Let one thing come to mind that you've stopped trying at: a conversation that never goes well, a habit you keep failing to start, a hope you put down.
Hold it next to Simon's sentence: I've worked all night and caught nothing, but I'll let down the net. If you pray, offer the trying to God.

wordCard.voice: Draught. An old word for a catch of fish: what filled Simon's nets when he tried once more at Jesus's word.

orig.note: Latin, from the Vulgate: lead out into the deep. John Paul II made it a motto for the new millennium.

carryVoice: Your line: but at thy word. Not sure it'll work, and letting down the net anyway. Six days into week five.
